parts.title: One Click In, Many Steps Out: The Hidden Friction of Subscriptions
parts.part1:
Starting a subscription often feels like an open door. One click, and you are inside.

Leaving can feel very different. The path may include extra screens, a phone call, or messages asking you to stay.

This gap has a name: sludge.

Richard H. Thaler discussed the idea in his 2018 *Science* article, “Nudge, not sludge.” A nudge helps people make a useful choice. Sludge adds friction when people try to do what they already want to do. For someone who no longer wants a subscription, that friction may stand between “cancel” and “cancelled.”

A 2025 paper for the European Association of Cognitive Ergonomics annual conference examined dark patterns in subscription cancellation. The study used a review and a user experiment. It also analyzed six services as case examples: The Economist, Bloomberg, Scribd, Adobe Creative Cloud, Amazon Prime, and Audible.
parts.part2:
The issue also reached US regulators.

On October 16, 2024, the Federal Trade Commission finalized its “Click-to-Cancel” rule. It covered automatic renewals, free trials that become paid plans, and continuing product deliveries.

Its central idea was simple:

Leaving should be about as easy as joining.

Cancellation should also be available through the same kind of channel used to sign up. The FTC had received more than 16,000 public comments since its March 2023 proposal.

But the story did not end there.

On July 8, 2025, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the whole rule for procedural reasons. After that decision, FTC guidance said the narrower Negative Option Rule from the 1973 era returned. The broad click-to-cancel standard was finalized—but it is not now in force.
parts.point_one_body: The 2025 study first identified 58 dark patterns in academic and grey literature. It then standardized them into 44 patterns across 10 categories. These included complexity, misleading interfaces, forced continuation, retention efforts, and mental overload. Cancellation trouble is not just one annoying button.
parts.point_two_heading: A cancel button is only part of the contract
parts.point_two_body: The FTC rule went beyond the final click. It also called for clear key terms before billing, separate and sufficient consent, no false statements about important facts, and consent records kept for at least three years. An easy exit was part of a wider plan for informed agreement.
parts.in_one_line: A subscription can begin with a tap, yet end in a maze. The debate over sludge asks a plain question: if joining is easy, why should leaving be hard?

parts.title: One Click In, a Maze Out: Why Subscriptions Can Be Hard to Cancel
parts.part1:
Starting a subscription can feel like walking through an open door.

A free trial appears. The price is clear. A few clicks later, the service is running.

Then you try to leave.

The door is no longer easy to find. There may be more pages, confusing choices, requests to stay, or even a phone call. No single step looks huge. Together, however, they can make the exit feel heavy.

This kind of friction has a name: sludge.

In choice design, sludge means barriers that make it harder for people to do what they want or what helps them. For a customer who no longer wants a subscription, a difficult exit can fit this idea. Researchers also study these screens as dark patterns.

The U.S. Federal Trade Commission tried to change this structure.
parts.part2:
On October 16, 2024, it finalized its Click-to-Cancel rule. It covered auto-renewing subscriptions, free trials that become paid plans, and continuing product deliveries.

Its main message was simple:

Canceling should be about as easy as signing up.

If someone joined online, there should be a simple online way to leave. The rule also called for clear key terms, separate consent, no false statements about important facts, and consent records kept for at least three years.

The plan followed a March 2023 proposal and more than 16,000 public comments.

But the legal story changed.

On July 8, 2025, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals canceled the full 2024 rule because of problems with the rule-making process. This followed a challenge from industry groups.

After that decision, FTC guidance returned to the narrower Negative Option Rule from the 1973 era. The broad Click-to-Cancel rule is therefore no longer in place.
parts.point_one_heading: The real cost is the whole journey
parts.point_one_body: The useful question is not only, “Can I cancel?” It is also, “How much work does canceling demand?” Richard H. Thaler’s 2018 *Science* article, “Nudge, not sludge,” gives this burden a useful name. The idea looks at the full exit journey, not only the final button.
parts.point_two_body: A 2025 conference study used a review and a user experiment. It identified 58 dark-pattern types, then created a system of 44 patterns in 10 groups. It used six services as cases: The Economist, Bloomberg, Scribd, Adobe Creative Cloud, Amazon Prime, and Audible.
parts.in_one_line: The entrance to a subscription may be wide and bright, while the exit is hidden behind friction—and the U.S. attempt to make both doors equally easy did not survive.
